RagShortTexts: Livestock sickness costs food, draught power and dues; its cause may be disputed.
Nursing animals, disposing of carcasses and replacing oxen consume household resources.

Variants.Content:
When an ox or horse suddenly collapses, a household loses more than a saleable animal. Oxen pull ploughs and carts, dairy animals feed children, and dead breeding females mean fewer young next season. Carers recognise poor appetite, fever, swelling or weakness without necessarily knowing the cause. Neighbours dispute bad fodder, water, weather or ill fortune and may seek an experienced herder or cleric.

Water, fodder, shelter and someone to watch a sick beast must be found. A carcass raises problems of removal, hides, meat and filth. Selling a failing animal can provoke a buyer, while mixing borrowed oxen with household stock complicates compensation. A neighbour lending draught power may save a sowing season, but fodder costs and responsibility for another death still need agreement.
After oxen die, collecting unchanged grain rents can consume seed. Estate stewards must consider surviving draught animals, arrears and loans of beasts, rather than treat deaths only as a cash loss.
A sick packhorse puts its load on other animals or human backs. Travelers judge whether it can stand and drink, then decide whether to halt, unload or leave someone to care for it.
A poor household may repay a borrowed plough animal with labour or grain. Nursing costs field work as well, and neighbours lend according to trust and their own spare capacity.
